about: Narration for the ArchitectureTour scene in scenes.py, one entry per step. scripts/voiceover.py turns each into docs/animations/voice/<id>.mp3; the scene waits for each clip. Change the words here, then run scripts/voiceover.py and docs/build.sh ArchitectureTour. 'covers' lists the overview diagram's blocks (architecture.md) the video shows, and 'planned' the dashed ones; scripts/check-docs.py fails when the diagram and these disagree.

steps.text: This is the gameRobotics architecture, built up one block at a time. Solid borders are running today. Dashed borders are planned.

At the centre is gamerobotd, the daemon, written in Rust. Its control loop ticks fifty times a second. Each tick, the controller and MotionCore turn what the robot wants into smooth joint targets, and Safety is the only thing allowed to write to the motors.

The loop talks to a body through one seam, called RobotIo. Today that body is the simulator: MuJoCo, with measured servo models, over a TCP socket, once per tick. On real hardware, the same seam becomes a servo driver, and nothing above it changes.
Everything else reaches the daemon through its API: JSON-RPC, over a local socket.

Apps are written in Python. The Runner hosts behaviours, like smooth follow, cat gaze, keep distance and mimic tilt. Each body part has one owner at a time, and the Runner sends the daemon intents, such as look at this point, up to fifty times a second.
Perception is its own process. face cam reads the webcam, finds your face with MediaPipe, and sends where it is to the app, about thirty times a second.
The simulator draws the robot in a viewer, and the app adds your face and the robot's line of sight, so you can see what it's thinking.
On top are the tools. gamerobotctl pokes the daemon directly. The gamerobotics command starts every process in order, watches their health, and stops them together.

Next comes the addressable API: a WebSocket on the daemon, a publisher that streams state and timing, and control and status APIs for the app and supervisor. Then a Tauri dashboard, like Reachy Mini's, built only on those APIs. And the servo driver, for the real robot.
That is the key rule. Every client talks to the robot by address, never by being on the same machine. So moving from a laptop to a robot with its own Pi is a new address, not a rewrite.
